steps.en: What you see: The aortic cusps look calcified and bright with restricted systolic opening. The left ventricular wall thickens while the cavity stays normal in size. Continuous wave Doppler down the outflow shows a high peak velocity with a late peaking envelope. In severe disease the valve area by continuity falls below 1.0 sq cm.

Normal values with units: Peak aortic velocity. Mild below 3 m per s. Moderate 3 to 4 m per s. Severe 4 m per s or more.. Source: ASE and EACVI 2017 valvular stenosis guideline, section on aortic stenosis quantitation
Mean transaortic gradient. Mild below 20 mmHg. Moderate 20 to 40 mmHg. Severe 40 mmHg or more.. Source: ASE and EACVI 2017 valvular stenosis guideline, section on aortic stenosis quantitation

Aortic valve area by continuity. Mild above 1.5 sq cm. Moderate 1.0 to 1.5 sq cm. Severe 1.0 sq cm or less. Outflow area times outflow velocity time integral divided by aortic velocity time integral.. Source: ASE and EACVI 2017 valvular stenosis guideline, section on the continuity equation

Dimensionless index. Outflow velocity divided by aortic velocity. Below 0.25 supports severe stenosis independent of outflow size.. Source: ASE and EACVI 2017 valvular stenosis guideline, section on aortic stenosis quantitation

ECG and heart sound correlation ecg: Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain in lateral leads marks chronic pressure load. Left axis deviation follows in advanced disease. Atrial fibrillation appears late when the left atrium dilates.

ECG and heart sound correlation sounds: A harsh ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiates to the carotids. The second sound softens as cusp mobility falls. A fourth sound marks the stiff filling ventricle.

What to report: Peak velocity, mean gradient and valve area with the windows used and blood pressure at the time
Outflow diameter with the velocity time integrals for audit of the continuity result
Wall thickness, ejection fraction and aortic root size
Symptoms of angina, syncope or breathlessness with the grade
Red flags needing urgent referral: Syncope, angina or breathlessness with severe stenosis, needs urgent valve team review
Ejection fraction below 50 percent with severe stenosis, needs prompt surgical review
Rheumatic aortic disease in a young Indian patient with combined mitral disease, needs urgent combined valve assessment
Pitfalls: Low flow states underread gradients, so check stroke volume index and consider dobutamine assessment on referral.
Hypertension raises afterload and lowers gradients, so record blood pressure with every study.
Bicuspid valves calcify early and read worse in short axis, so count cusps in systole before grading.

todo.en: How to get it on the probe, step by step: Start in the parasternal long axis and assess cusp thickness, brightness and opening in systole.
Measure the outflow tract diameter at the leaflet hinge points in mid systole.
Move to the apical five chamber view and align the beam as parallel to flow as possible.
Record pulsed wave Doppler just below the valve for the outflow velocity time integral.
Record continuous wave Doppler through the valve from apex, right parasternal and suprasternal windows and keep the highest clean envelope.

Common mistakes and how to correct them: Underreading velocity with an off axis beam from the apex alone. Fix: Interrogate from apex, right parasternal and suprasternal windows and keep the highest complete envelope.
Measuring the outflow diameter too large and overestimating valve area. Fix: Measure inner edge to inner edge exactly at the hinges in systole, since a 1 mm error squares in the area.
Calling severe stenosis from gradients alone in anaemia, fever or a small aortic root. Fix: Check pressure recovery in a small root and index the area to body surface area before calling severe.

q.en: Which set meets severe aortic stenosis criteria?

o.en: Peak velocity 2.5 m per s with mean gradient 15 mmHg
Peak velocity 4.5 m per s with mean gradient 48 mmHg
Peak velocity 3.2 m per s with mean gradient 25 mmHg

why.en: Severe needs peak velocity of 4 m per s or more with mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more and area of 1.0 sq cm or less.

q.en: How do you avoid missing the true peak velocity?

o.en: Keep the highest complete envelope from apex, right parasternal and suprasternal views

why.en: The beam must parallel flow, and the best window varies, so interrogate all three and keep the highest clean signal.

q.en: Which pattern warns of low gradient severe stenosis that gradients alone miss?

o.en: A bicuspid valve in a teenager
Low gradient with low stroke volume and poor ejection fraction

why.en: A weak pump ejects too little to generate gradients, so valve area and stroke volume index decide, with dobutamine assessment on referral.

q.en: Syncope occurs with a harsh ejection murmur and severe echo gradients. What next?

o.en: Urgent valve team review for syncope with severe stenosis
Reassurance that murmurs are always innocent

why.en: Syncope with severe stenosis marks high sudden death risk and needs urgent valve team review.
